Series::real¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series Series::real() const

What It Does¶

Returns the real part of each element.

For a complex input the result is a real-valued Series of the same shape: Complex64 yields float32, Complex128 yields float64. For an input that is already real, real() returns the values unchanged (a plain copy), so it is safe to call in dtype-agnostic code.

real() pairs with imag(): together they split a complex series into its two real components, and pluss::series::complex recombines them.

Reading The Result¶

real() changes the number representation, not the arrangement of the data. A [rows, columns] complex series produces a [rows, columns] real series with the same element positions. It does not flatten, reduce, compute a magnitude, or discard rows whose imaginary part is zero.

This distinction matters when a complex calculation is followed by ordinary data work. Extracting real() gives a standalone real series that can be filtered, aggregated, or exported without carrying a complex dtype. The source is not modified, and the result owns independent storage.

Parameters¶

None.

Returns¶

Series The real component. Shape is preserved. The dtype is the real counterpart of a complex input (Complex64 -> float32, Complex128 -> float64), or the input dtype unchanged when the input is already real.

Gradient¶

real() is differentiable. For a real input it is the identity, so the sensitivity passes straight through. For a complex input the backward lifts the real cotangent back into the complex plane with a zero imaginary part (the Wirtinger convention), so a reverse pass through z.real() accumulates grad + 0j into z.

Examples¶

Example 1. The real part of a complex series. Here the series is assembled from its two real components with pluss::series::complex, so real() simply hands back the first of them.

auto z = pluss::series::complex(
    pluss::make_series({3.0f, -1.0f, 0.0f, 0.0f}),   // real parts
    pluss::make_series({4.0f,  0.0f, 2.0f, 0.0f}));  // imaginary parts

pluss::series::print(std::cout, z.real()) << "\n";

Output¶

Series(shape=[4], strides=[1], dtype=float32, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[3.0000, -1.0000, 0.0000, 0.0000]

The same series could be written directly from std::complex literals — pluss::make_series({std::complex<float>{3, 4}, {-1, 0}, {0, 2}, {0, 0}}) — and either form is idiomatic.

Example 2. On a real input real() returns the values unchanged.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({-3.0, 0.0, 2.5}).real()
) << "\n";

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[-3.0000, 0.0000, 2.5000]

Example 3. On a real leaf the backward is the identity.

auto a = pluss::make_series({2.0, -1.0});
a.tracks_slope_(true);
a.real().sum().reverse();

pluss::series::print(std::cout, a.sensitivity()) << "\n";

Output¶

Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[1.0000, 1.0000]

Example 4. Shape is preserved for matrices. Each output cell is the first Cartesian coordinate of the complex value in the corresponding input cell.

auto z = pluss::series::complex(
    pluss::make_series({{3.0f, -1.0f}, {0.0f, 0.0f}}),
    pluss::make_series({{4.0f,  0.0f}, {2.0f, 0.0f}}));
pluss::series::print(std::cout, z.real()) << "\n";

Output¶

Series(shape=[2,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=float32, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=
⎡  3.0000 -1.0000 ⎤
⎣  0.0000  0.0000 ⎦

Example 5. real() and imag() form a lossless Cartesian round-trip when they are recombined at the matching complex precision.

auto z = pluss::series::complex(
    pluss::make_series({{3.0f, -1.0f}, {0.0f, 0.0f}}),
    pluss::make_series({{4.0f,  0.0f}, {2.0f, 0.0f}}));
auto rebuilt = pluss::series::complex(z.real(), z.imag());
pluss::series::print(std::cout, rebuilt) << "\n";

Output¶

Series(shape=[2,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=complex64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=
⎡ (3.0000+4.0000j) (-1.0000+0.0000j) ⎤
⎣ (0.0000+2.0000j)  (0.0000+0.0000j) ⎦

Example 6. On a tracked complex series, summing the real component lifts each unit output sensitivity back as 1 + 0j. This shows that the imaginary input coordinate does not influence a real-component objective.

auto z = pluss::series::complex(
    pluss::make_series({{3.0f, -1.0f}, {0.0f, 0.0f}}),
    pluss::make_series({{4.0f,  0.0f}, {2.0f, 0.0f}}));
z.tracks_slope_(true);
z.real().sum().reverse();
pluss::series::print(std::cout, z.sensitivity()) << "\n";

Output¶

Series(shape=[2,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=complex64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=
⎡ (1.0000+0.0000j) (1.0000+0.0000j) ⎤
⎣ (1.0000+0.0000j) (1.0000+0.0000j) ⎦

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • The result dtype changes for a complex input: Complex64 gives float32, not float64. Convert with to() if you need a specific precision.

  • real() on a real series is a copy, not a view; mutating the result does not touch the source.

  • real() is not abs(). For 3 + 4j, the real component is 3, while the magnitude is 5.

  • To rebuild a complex series from parts, use pluss::series::complex, not arithmetic on real() / imag().

Summary¶

real() is the real component of each element:

  • complex in, real out (Complex64 -> float32, Complex128 -> float64)

  • identity on a real input

  • differentiable; the backward carries a zero imaginary part on the complex path

  • the counterpart of imag()

See Also¶

  • Series::imag: the imaginary component.

  • Series::conj: the complex conjugate, real - imag * i.

  • Series::angle: the phase.

  • pluss::series::complex: build a complex series from real and imaginary parts.
